document.title: Terrorism: Near Eastern Groups and State Sponsors, 2001
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Terrorism and U.S. Policy
document.note: [Unclassified] CRS study published September 10, 2001. It profiles many terrorist groups (radical Islamic groups including Al-Qaida, radical Jewish, leftwing and nationalist groups) and state sponsorship by Iran, Syria, Libya, Sudan and Iraq. It also covers countering terrorism in the region. The summary notes a decline in state sponsorship and a rise in the threat from Usama bin Ladin's independent network.

key_claims: Bin Ladin's independently financed network, with safe haven in Afghanistan, poses an increasingly significant threat to U.S. interests as state sponsorship of terrorism declines.
Bin Ladin's primary goals are to oust pro-U.S. Middle East regimes and remove U.S. troops from the region; past plotting suggests intent to strike inside the U.S.
Pakistani Kashmir groups are covered because of alleged connections to the bin Ladin network and the Taliban.
Al-Qa'ida was designated an FTO on August 21, 1998 and rated 'Extremely High' in activity.
Hizballah receives substantial support from Iran and Syria, about $100 million per year from Iran.
Hizballah has demonstrated global reach, blamed for Buenos Aires bombings, and is helping Palestinian groups against Israel.
Iran gives Hizballah about $100 million per year, with Syria permitting arms transit via Damascus airport.
Hamas and PIJ escalated suicide bombings after September 2000, with Iran as the key sponsor, closer to PIJ.
Exiled Islamic Group and Al-Jihad factions have gravitated to bin Ladin, with Zawahiri, Rifai Taha Musa and Mohammad Atef as top lieutenants.
Al-Qaida is a coalition of Arab Afghan veterans and militant groups (Egyptian, Algerian, HuM, IMU, Saudi opposition), financed by bin Ladin's fortune of about $300 million.
The Taliban give bin Ladin safehaven but he is not acting on their behalf, and they have refused extradition.
Bin Ladin's network is linked to attacks including the 1998 embassy bombings and plots against Americans, with USS Cole suspected.
After the 1998 US strikes the Taliban tried to dissociate from bin Ladin but refused repeated US extradition requests.
Bin Ladin has about $300 million in personal assets and funds up to 3,000 militants with cells in dozens of countries.
Zawahiri and Atef are viewed as potential successors; Zawahiri is bin Ladin's closest adviser.
HUM is allied with or part of bin Ladin's network; Khalil signed the Feb 1998 fatwa, and the Feb 2000 leadership move to Kashmiri may signal distancing.
JEM, a HUM splinter formed by Masood Azhar, is politically aligned with bin Ladin, the Taliban and JUI and probably receives bin Ladin funds.
IMU leaders Yuldashev and Namangani reportedly have safehaven in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, and bin Ladin may fund the IMU.
Exiled GIA members gravitated to bin Ladin's network and the Dec 1999 LAX plot involved a GIA-linked cell from Canada.
Lashkar-e-Jhangvi declared itself an ally of bin Ladin; Lashkar-e-Tayyiba is one of the three largest Kashmir groups, run through the MDI.
Islamic Army of Aden members are suspected of links to bin Ladin, though some experts say the group as a whole is not closely linked to him and is unlikely to have carried out the USS Cole attack.

The Yemeni government does not support radical Islamists as policy but has tolerated extremists in areas under tenuous control, and U.S. officials were unsatisfied with its Cole investigation cooperation.
Syria is the chief backer of the PFLP-GC, which also receives Iranian financial assistance, and the PFLP and DFLP are headquartered in Syria.
The PFLP-GC allegedly was approached by Iran to bomb a U.S. jet and may have handed the operation to Libya, leading to Pan Am 103.
Abu Nidal, expelled successively from Iraq, Syria, Libya and Egypt, was in Iraq as of 2001 with no hard evidence that he was reviving his network.
Israel alleged that Fatah, the Tanzim and Force 17 encouraged violence after September 2000, prompting calls in Congress to designate them as FTOs.
Kach and Kahane Chai were declared terrorist organizations by Israel after supporting Goldstein's 1994 Hebron attack; Rabin's assassin Yigal Amir was not a formal member of either group.
The PKK is transitioning from guerrilla group to political movement after Ocalan's 1999 capture and call to cease armed operations, though ~5,000 fighters remain in Iran and northern Iraq.
State Department attributes Iranian terrorism support to the Revolutionary Guard and Ministry of Intelligence and Security rather than the Iranian government as a whole.
DOJ's June 2001 indictments of 14 people allege Iranian security personnel inspired and supervised the 1996 Khobar Towers bombing carried out by Saudi Hizballah.
Syria continues to allow Iranian resupply of Hizballah via Damascus and hosts Hamas, while generally honoring its pledge to Turkey on the PKK.
Libya's Pan Am 103 handover and distancing from Palestinian groups prompted review of its listing, but conviction of al-Megrahi reinforced suspicion of Qadhafi's role.
Sudan is closest to removal from the terrorism list; Turabi, patron of ties to Al Qaida and others, was sidelined in 1999 and arrested in 2001.
The 1998 al-Shifa strike, tied to bin Ladin allegedly, was widely seen as a tacit error after US unfroze the owner's assets in 1999.
The 1998 US strikes did not lead the Taliban to expel bin Ladin nor deter his network.
The US designated the Taliban under EO 13129 and pushed UNSCR 1267 and 1333 over its harboring of bin Ladin.
Afghanistan has been on the 'not cooperating' list since 1997 but never the terrorism list, to avoid implying recognition of the Taliban.
Pakistan was seen as a candidate for the terrorism or 'not cooperating' list but was spared to avoid alienating it.
Pakistan assisted US captures of Ramzi Yusuf and Mir Aimal Kansi.
Iraq hosts Abu Nidal, the PLF and the PMOI/NLA, but reduced PMOI support as ties with Iran improved.
The US has expanded counterterrorism dialogue with Russia and Central Asian states in cooperating against the bin Ladin network.
Since 1999 the State Department has hosted annual multilateral conferences on terrorism from Afghanistan.
US-provided detection equipment helped Uzbekistan seize radioactive material bound for Pakistan in April 2000.
Some observers allege Middle Eastern groups run fundraising networks in the US via charities and institutes, which the groups deny.
Stronger law enforcement powers might have helped foil the alleged millennium Los Angeles airport plot by bin Ladin supporters.
